name: PT Merck Tbk

frontmatter.title: Merck Tbk: a dated manufacturing contract, a prescription franchise, and a price that pays for neither
frontmatter.summary: MERK's repriced P&G manufacturing contract ends on 31 December 2027 and takes about a third of sales with it. On a ten-year explicit DCF with an explicit terminal value, the prescription business and the net cash are worth well above the price; on the June 2026 balance sheet the market pays about six and a half times post-contract EBITDA, which is cheap but not free. BUY, with the parent's control the reason it stays cheap.
thesis: The P&G supply price rose 98.0% under the current manufacturing agreement [S2], so FY2026E and FY2027E are contractually protected cash, and the contract ends on 31 December 2027 [S5].

The tolling book is the -31.4% step in FY2028E revenue, roughly a third of FY2027E sales on our own derivation from the sourced price step, and it goes; what remains is the prescription franchise that grew 7.7% against a market that grew 6.2% [S2].

At the price the market pays 8.9x the earnings of the first post-contract year [S0]. The engine prints 3.7x for post-contract EBITDA, but that number credits FY2028E forecast net cash; on the 30 June 2026 balance sheet the same EBITDA is six and a half times and EBIT is just under seven times, so the shares are cheap for a prescription franchise but not the giveaway the forward figure implies.
Net cash of IDR-349.6bn is a fifth of the market value [S0]; a minority reaches it through the dividend, which the board has kept at about half of profit [S3].

Our target is Rp4,704, a 46.0% total return including the dividend, on a DCF that runs ten explicit years and then a terminal growth rate of 4.0%; the terminal value is 44.2% of enterprise value — not nothing, and not a perpetuity of peak tolling profit.

The reason the shares stay cheap is structural: a free float the registry puts at 12.5%, a controlling parent whose pack stake line of 91.3% is counted on a different definition, and 104,688,444 rupiah a day traded [S0].

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results and the FY2026 dividend declaration, the first clean read on the repriced contract margin
Philippines export shipments of the oral antidiabetic portfolio from the Pasar Rebo plant
End of the P&G manufacturing agreement, the single largest identifiable earnings event for the name
FY2027 general meeting and dividend, the last declaration before the contract cliff

blocks.text: We initiate on PT Merck Tbk with a **BUY** rating and a target of Rp4,704, a total return of 46.0% including the dividend expected in the window from the last close of Rp3,490. The target is the probability-weighted fundamental value of Rp5,880, rolled forward at the cost of equity, less the dividend paid in the window, and cut 20% for thin traded volume; three-month average daily traded value is 104,688,444 rupiah [S0]. One dating convention has to be stated because it changes how the return should be read: the engine discounts from the 30 June 2026 balance-sheet date, so the value is struck at that date and the one-year roll-forward dates the target to about 30 June 2027, not to twelve months from the 6 November 2026 price [S0]. Against that price the target is struck only about eight months forward, so the 46.0% total return annualises to materially more than the headline number; we keep the engine convention and attach the date rather than restate it.

The variant view is not that this is a quality compounder. It is that the market has done the post-contract arithmetic and then applied a control discount large enough to assume the remaining business is worth little. At Rp3,490 the shares change hands on 4.2x the last full contract year's earnings and 8.9x the first post-contract year's [S0]. The post-contract multiple depends on which balance sheet carries the enterprise value, and the two are not interchangeable. The engine prints 3.7x because it nets the cash the business is forecast to hold by FY2028E, cash not yet earned; on the 30 June 2026 balance sheet, where net cash is about a fifth of the market value, the same FY2028E EBITDA is six and a half times and the same operating profit is just under seven times [S0]. That is not a price that ignores the cliff; it is a price that has taken the cliff and then a discount on top for who owns the company — cheap, but not the giveaway the forward figure implies.

The business is in two halves with the same end date. PT Merck Tbk manufactures consumer-health products for Procter & Gamble under a manufacturing supply agreement that runs to 31 December 2027 and is not being renewed; management has said it will stop producing consumer-health goods when the agreement lapses and will concentrate on prescription medicines [S5][S6]. In the same public expose the company disclosed that the supply price under the newest agreement rose 98.0%, which is what turned a thin-margin tolling book into the profit engine behind the step change in group margins and the 396% jump in first-half net profit [S2].

Our target rests on three sourced drivers, in order of weight. First, the tolling cash flow of FY2026E and FY2027E, which is protected by the contract and already visible in the reported first half [S2]. Second, net cash: on the 30 June 2026 balance sheet cash exceeds borrowings, and we carry it net in the valuation [S0]. The company's own leverage measure of 0.3x with a current ratio of 5.0x is a total-liabilities-to-equity ratio, not a borrowings figure, and we do not use it as evidence of net cash [S5]. Third, a prescription franchise that grew 7.7% in the latest half against a market that grew 6.2% and an ethical segment that grew 6.5% [S2]. The reverse DCF later in this section shows what the price implies: the same model run backwards needs revenue growth -14.3% against our path in every forecast year — which puts implied FY2027E growth at -9.3% versus the 5.0% we assume — a path worse than our bear case, for a business whose prescription sales have compounded through the cycle [S0].

What would change our mind is not a bad quarter. It is evidence that the parent intends to take the Indonesian entity private or to strip the prescription portfolio out of it, that transfer prices on imported biotech products are being moved against minorities, or that the export plan stalls. The free float is 12.5% on the registry's basis while the pack's insider line is 91.3% on a different one — the two are not additive, and the business section reconciles them — and three-month average daily traded value is only about 104,688,444 rupiah a day, so position size is a real constraint on who can own this at all; we return to that in the risks section [S0].

PT Merck Tbk is the Indonesian listed vehicle of Merck KGaA. The company manufactures, imports and distributes prescription pharmaceuticals and, until the end of 2027, manufactures consumer-health products for Procter & Gamble. Its products cover cardiovascular, metabolic, oncology, endocrinology, fertility and neurodegenerative therapy areas, and it also runs office and property leasing from its Jakarta site [S0]. The registered address is on Jalan TB Simatupang in East Jakarta and the manufacturing plant sits in Pasar Rebo [S0][S5].

The revenue model has two very different halves. The prescription business is a mix of imported finished biotech products and in-house manufacture: management disclosed that about 60.0% percent of Healthcare sales come from imported biotechnology products and about 40.0% from products the company makes itself [S2][S6]. The consumer-health half is a toll-manufacturing arrangement: Merck produces P&G goods at Pasar Rebo and sells them to P&G under a manufacturing supply agreement, rather than owning the brands. That agreement expires on 31 December 2027 and the company has decided not to continue consumer-health production afterwards [S5].

The strategic pivot is explicit and dated. In the October 2026 public expose management said the Pasar Rebo plant will serve domestic prescription demand and be developed as an export base for Asia, starting with the Philippines in 2026 and extending to Hong Kong, Singapore, Brunei, Malaysia and Thailand over 2027 to 2029, with Glucophage XR, Glucophage IR, Glucovance and Concor as the lead products [S6]. The same presentation flagged Bavencio, Mavenclad and the launch of TEPMETKO for lung cancer as the domestic growth drivers, and said the company is assessing additional products from the parent's SpringWorks acquisition for the Indonesian market [S2].

Scale and position are modest but not marginal. Merck describes itself as eighth among foreign pharmaceutical companies in Indonesia by sales, and its first-half growth of 7.7% outpaced both the total market at 6.2% and the ethical segment at 6.5% [S2]. The company employed roughly 331.0 people at the last count [S0], which is small for a manufacturer with a plant, a national distribution footprint and a hospital-facing sales force; it is consistent with a portfolio company that runs a lean commercial organisation on top of group-manufactured and group-imported products rather than a full-research pharmaceutical house.

One number needs defining, because it carries the whole forecast. The 7.7% the company quotes is its own underlying growth, the measure it sets against the 6.2% total market and the 6.5% ethical segment in the same presentation [S2]. It is not total revenue growth. The two are consistent, and the arithmetic is the story of this name: a 98.0% step in the P&G supply price applied to a tolling book that was about a quarter of sales at the old price adds roughly a quarter to group revenue on flat volume, so underlying growth of 7.7% plus the contract re-pricing lands close to the first-half revenue increase the data pack reports [S2][S0]. We therefore use 7.7% as the prescription growth rate and never as group revenue growth; the group number in FY2026E is the trailing twelve months, which already contains the price step.

The controlling shareholder is Merck Holding GmbH, part of Merck KGaA of Darmstadt. Three ownership figures are in circulation and they are not additive. The pack's insider line is 91.3%, its institution line is 2.5%, and the house registry puts the free float at 12.5% [S0]. The insider line counts shares reported by insiders and affiliates, the float is the registry's estimate of shares that actually trade, and the institution line is a separate survey; adding them produces an impossible total, which the earlier draft did. What is not in doubt is the control position: one shareholder holds the overwhelming majority of the votes and the float is about an eighth of the shares. We use the registry float for the liquidity work and never sum the lines. That ownership structure matters more than usual here because the parent is simultaneously the supplier of the imported biotech portfolio, the licensor of the brands, and the controlling vote. The governance section treats the related-party exposure in detail.

PT Merck Tbk has been listed since the early years of the Jakarta exchange and for decades was known
to Indonesian investors as a consumer-health franchise built on vitamin and tonic brands. The global
parent's decision to exit consumer health reshaped the local entity into a prescription-led business
with a manufacturing service contract attached, which is the structure we analyse today.

The Indonesian pharmaceutical market grew 6.2% in the first half of 2026, with the ethical or prescription segment growing 6.5%, according to the market data presented at the company's public expose [S2]. That is a mid-single-digit nominal growth market, roughly in line with Indonesian nominal growth less the deflator drag that a price-controlled, heavily reimbursed healthcare market carries. Within it, the multinational segment where Merck competes is the premium end: imported biologics and originator molecules priced above local generics, sold through hospitals and specialists rather than through pharmacy shelves [S2].

Demand is structurally supported by the national health insurance scheme, which underwrites prescription volumes, and by a population with a rising metabolic disease burden. That is exactly where Merck's portfolio sits: the export plan is built on oral antidiabetics such as Glucophage and Glucovance, and the domestic launch emphasis is oncology and multiple sclerosis [S6][S2]. The offsetting force is price: the reimbursed market is a negotiated one, and imported products are exposed to rupiah weakness because about 60.0% of Healthcare sales are imported finished goods whose cost is dollar-denominated while the selling price is rupiah [S2][S6]. That is a margin channel rather than a demand channel, and it is the single most important industry variable for this name.

Competition is layered. The scale leader in listed Indonesian pharma is Kalbe Farma, which we rate BUY and which competes across prescription, consumer and distribution; Darya-Varia and Kimia Farma, both of which we rate SELL, compete in prescription and in the state-owned channel respectively; Sido Muncul and Soho Global Health compete in herbal and consumer health. Merck does not compete with any of them on breadth. It competes on a narrow set of originator molecules, on hospital relationships, and on the fact that it can manufacture to Merck KGaA's quality standard in-country. That is a defensible niche, not a franchise with pricing power over the whole market [S2].

Five-forces view. Supplier power is high and unusually concentrated: the parent supplies the imported portfolio and sets the transfer price, which is a structural feature rather than a negotiating outcome [S2][S6]. Buyer power is moderate to high in the reimbursed channel, where formulary decisions and price negotiation sit with payers, and low in the private specialist channel where originator brands carry weight. Threat of new entry is low for biologics and high for generics, which is why the portfolio skews to the former. Substitution is a live risk in diabetes and cardiovascular therapy, where local generics are clinically acceptable and much cheaper. Rivalry is intense at the molecular level, but a stable position as the eighth foreign player by sales suggests the company is not losing ground [S2].

The moat question is the one the valuation card forces us to answer. Merck's advantage is not a network effect or a switching cost; it is a regulatory and quality barrier to manufacturing certain originator products locally, plus a brand relationship with prescribers that comes from the parent's global clinical data. We do not see evidence that this moat is widening. The honest description is a narrow moat that supports mid-single-digit growth and returns above the cost of capital, and no more. The tolling contract was never a moat at all: it was a commercial arrangement with a fixed end date, which is precisely why we treat its cash flow as a finite annuity rather than as earnings to capitalise [S5].

The external influences that matter are the rupiah, the reimbursed-price regime and the parent's global portfolio decisions. The house macro deck has the rupiah at 18,350 against a spot of 17,968 and drifting to 19,000 in the long run, which is the direction that hurts this company: a weaker rupiah raises the cost of the imported majority of the portfolio and compresses gross margin unless the company can reprice [S6]. We do not shock it separately in the scenarios because it is already in the discount rate and in the cost base; we do state it as a named risk in the risk section, and it is the reason we hold the post-contract gross margin at the prescription-only level rather than above it.

The sector view we are working against is that Indonesian pharmaceutical margins are under structural pressure, and we take it seriously rather than routing around it. The peers we cover show the two mechanisms: a distribution-led model whose gross margin is set by the mix of generics it pushes, and an originator-led model whose margin is set by the price it can hold in a reimbursed channel. Merck sits in the second camp and inherits the second problem. Its answer is to manufacture locally what it currently imports, which cuts the dollar cost of goods and is partly a hedge against exactly the rupiah path above [S6]. What the sector view does not support is extrapolating the FY2025 and FY2026 margins: those are the contract re-pricing, a price event on a fixed volume, and they fade with the contract. That is why our post-contract margin sits at the prescription-only level and not above it. Parent-level decisions are the third channel: the SpringWorks acquisition gives the group new oncology assets that could be routed through Indonesia, and the same relationship could equally route products elsewhere in Asia [S2].

FY2025 was a step-change year. Revenue reached IDR1,200.7bn, up from IDR1,036.7bn, operating profit rose to IDR321.4bn from IDR193.9bn, and net profit reached IDR243.9bn from IDR153.5bn [S3][S0]. The company attributes the increase to higher sales and better manufacturing economics, and disclosed in the 2026 public expose that the supply price under the newest manufacturing agreement rose 98.0%; the reported gross margin moved from 38.8% to 47.6% on that base [S3][S2].

That margin move is the analytical heart of the name, and it is why we treat the reported earnings with care rather than at face value. A cost-plus manufacturing agreement produces lumpy recognition: the quarterly pack shows a weak first half and a very strong fourth quarter in 2025, consistent with an annual true-up of the contractual margin rather than a demand event [S0]. We therefore model the contract years on an annual gross margin near 50.0% and 50.0%, and we do not extrapolate the fourth-quarter margin, which is the single most misleading number in the pack [S0].

Our forecast has four phases. FY2026E is not a fiscal year and we do not pretend it is: it is the trailing twelve months to 30 June 2026 the data pack carries, IDR1,350.8bn of revenue at its own 50.0% gross margin and IDR430.9bn of operating profit [S0]. The house rule is that the first forecast year reproduces the last actual at that year's prices, and this year the last actual is the twelve months that already contain two quarters of the repriced contract, so we take its economics as they are rather than haircutting them. FY2027E adds 5.0% as the contract runs its first clean calendar year at the new price [S5]. That is the sourced running rate, not a deliberately cautious mark: the prescription book carries the 7.7% company growth on roughly two-thirds of the year while the tolling volume is flat, and the composition reproduces the rate above [S2]. FY2028E removes the tolling book and revenue steps down to IDR972.9bn from IDR1,418.3bn before prescription growth resumes [S5][S6]. From FY2029E we carry 7.0% fading to 6.5% and 5.0% thereafter as the export programme scales [S6].

The size of the tolling book is disclosed in no source we could obtain, so we derive it from the sourced inputs instead of asserting a band. The supply price rose 98.0% [S2] while P&G volume slipped fractionally, so a book that was about a quarter of first-half 2025 sales at the old price became close to two-fifths of first-half 2026 sales at the new one [S2]. FY2027E, at IDR1,418.3bn, is the first clean full year at that price, which puts the tolling book at roughly a third of it. Removing that while the prescription business still grows 7.7% [S2] is what produces the -31.4% step. That is the base case and not the bear case: the earlier draft used a pre-price-step share and understated the cliff, and the bear scenario now takes the share higher rather than treating a third as a pessimistic outcome.

Costs and margins. SG&A ran at IDR249.9bn in FY2025, leaving an operating margin of 26.8%; in the contract years the same absolute cost base is spread over a much larger revenue pool, and we hold SG&A at IDR244.5bn and IDR258.1bn [S5][S6]. What happens to it after the cliff is the second largest judgement in the report, and it is not symmetric. The P&G agreement is a manufacturing supply agreement: P&G owns the brands and funds the commercial spend, Merck runs the plant [S5][S6]. The cost that leaves with it is therefore plant and supply-chain cost inside cost of goods, not the prescription detail force that sits in SG&A. Against prescription-only revenue, SG&A ran between a fifth and three-tenths of sales across FY2022A to FY2024A, and we hold the ratio at 26.5% from FY2028E, at the top of that observed range and flat thereafter. We do not claim operating leverage in the trough: the ratio is the cliff expressed as a cost line. The bull case is the only place where the cost block tied to the tolling book leaves alongside the revenue.

The Pasar Rebo impairment needs a period, and it has one. The IDR87.0bn write-down was booked in September 2026 [S5], after the 30 June 2026 balance sheet that closes our FY2026E base, so it is not stacked into a period whose revenue ends in June. It is a non-cash charge: it takes net book value to IDR75.0bn against an appraised market value of IDR93.0bn [S5], it reduces book value and equity, and it does not touch free cash flow. It is disclosed in the post-balance-sheet review in the valuation section rather than in the earnings path.

Cash flow and earnings quality. The figures below are the engine's free cash flow to the firm, which is the number the DCF discounts, not the data pack's own free-cash-flow line; the two differ on interest and on the treatment of leases and should not be read against each other. FY2024 is the year to be suspicious of: operating profit of IDR193.9bn converted to FCFF of only IDR22.0bn, because working capital absorbed IDR121.9bn as receivables and inventory grew ahead of revenue [S0]. FY2025 reversed it, with FCFF of IDR310.3bn against net profit of IDR243.9bn, helped by a working-capital release of IDR-77.9bn [S0]. Over three years the pattern is one of wider swings than a distributor should have, which we read as a contract-accounting artefact rather than as manipulation: there is no evidence of capitalised cost games, the balance sheet is almost unlevered, and the audit trail we could obtain is thin but shows nothing adverse. It does mean a single year's cash conversion should not be annualised, and it is a reason we value on a multi-year DCF rather than on a capitalised current-year free cash flow.

Balance sheet and capital allocation. Net debt is IDR-349.6bn at end-FY2025, which is to say net cash, with cash of IDR363.9bn and borrowings of IDR14.2bn [S0]. Equity is IDR975.7bn and return on equity was 27.4% on average equity, which is the basis the engine uses; on year-end equity the same profit gives a lower figure, and the first-half figure management quotes, 11.6%, is a half-year return not annualised [S2]. Capex is the least demanding line in the model at IDR15.9bn, consistent with a plant that is already built and, after the impairment, carried at IDR75.0bn [S0][S5]. Capital allocation is dividend-led: FY2025 declared IDR123.2bn, Rp275 per share, 50.5% of net profit after a higher payout in FY2024 [S3][S0]. No source we obtained contains dividend guidance for the transition, so the payout we carry, 50.0%, is our own assumption held flat through the cliff and tested in the bear case, not a company guide. If it is wrong it is wrong in the direction of the target: a board that cuts would keep more cash inside a company the market already values at a fraction of it.

Growth here is not manufactured by reinvestment. Capex of IDR23.0bn against operating profit of IDR430.9bn is a reinvestment rate in the low single digits, so the incremental return on invested capital is driven by portfolio mix and price rather than by new capital [S0]. That is the correct reading of a company whose plant is already built and partly written down: the compounding, such as it is, comes from selling more of the parent's molecules through an existing asset base, not from building new capacity [S6]. It also means the DCF is relatively insensitive to the capex assumption and highly sensitive to the revenue path, which is where we have concentrated our uncertainty.

We use a discounted cash flow to the firm as the primary method and, after this revision, the only weight-bearing method. The earlier draft put thirty percent on a forward earnings multiple and ten on an EV/EBITDA multiple. The engine can only compute those legs on last-twelve-month earnings, and for this company the last twelve months are H1-2026 plus H2-2025, a period in which the fourth quarter of 2025 alone carried the contractual true-up on the repriced tolling book. Capitalising that base and calling it a forward multiple is the precise error this report is written against, so the valuation is the DCF alone and the multiples appear below as cross-checks at the price. The choice of method follows the industry card and the shape of these cash flows: the asset base is small and largely written down, the earnings stream is contract-dated rather than cyclical, and the balance sheet is net cash, so a cash-flow model with an explicit cliff is the only construction that represents what is actually happening. A price-to-book approach would mislead because the plant has just been written down to IDR75.0bn and book value says nothing about the value of the imported portfolio [S5]. A lower weight on the DCF would need an earnings base that spans the cliff, and on the disclosures we have there is none.

The cost of capital is built from the house macro deck rather than from company history, and the build has one step the earlier draft left out. The engine starts from a risk-free rate of 7.4%, subtracts a sovereign default spread of 1.6%, adds the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the country risk premium of 2.5% to a levered beta of 0.71 — the pharmaceutical-sector default, relevered only trivially because the company is 1% debt-funded [S0] — and then adds a company premium of 0.5%. The subtraction is not a free lunch and it is not a double count: the ten-year rupiah yield already embeds sovereign credit risk, so removing the default spread from the risk-free rate and pricing country risk explicitly through the country premium counts that exposure once rather than twice. The consequence is that the mechanical result lands below the house's eleven-to-thirteen-per-cent band for rupiah cash flows, which is why we add the company premium: a controlled micro-cap with a float of about an eighth of the shares and a contract that ends in fourteen months should not be discounted at less than the band floor. That gives a cost of equity of 11.1% and a WACC of 11.0%, both at the bottom of the band rather than under it. We charge illiquidity once, in the 20% haircut the house limits require at this traded value, and not a second time in the discount rate. The company premium is the band-floor correction on the sovereign-spread convention, not a second charge for illiquidity, and the earlier draft was right that adding a liquidity premium to the cost of equity would double count. The test of that judgement is in the sensitivity table: with the cost of capital half a point higher the target still clears the price.

The DCF runs ten explicit forecast years to FY2035E and then an explicit terminal value. We state that plainly because the earlier version of this report claimed there was none: the horizon entry was read by the engine as a count of periods, the model ran for thousands of years, and what looked like a no-terminal-value DCF was a perpetuity in disguise. The terminal value is now 44.2% of the DCF's enterprise value of IDR2,274.5bn, growing at 4.0% nominal in rupiah from FY2036E, below the house cap and far below long-run Indonesian nominal growth. The remainder, the ten explicit years including the FY2028E trough, is worth a little more than the tail. Two things make the tail defensible rather than lazy. It capitalises the prescription franchise only, because the tolling book has gone by FY2028E and no part of the terminal value is a capitalised contract. And the multiple-survival test now runs the right way round: the terminal value implies an exit EV/EBIT of about nine and a half times FY2035E operating profit of IDR275.9bn — roughly two-fifths above the close-to-seven times operating profit at which the shares trade today on the 30 June 2026 net cash, and level with what our own target implies. That is multiple expansion relative to today's price, and the earlier draft said the opposite. We do not dress it up as a narrow-moat victory either: at 4.0% growth and an 11.0% WACC, that is the steady-state multiple the perpetuity arithmetic produces, so the tail is capitalised at growth rather than re-rated for a widening moat. The valuation card asks for excess returns to fade toward the cost of capital by year ten unless the moat widens, and the industry section says this moat is narrow and not widening. The engine has no explicit ROIC-fade line, so we meet the discipline the only honest way available: we say that the tail carries the assumption, and we test it. Repricing the terminal value at today's post-contract multiple instead of the steady-state multiple takes about a tenth off the target and still leaves it above the price, cutting the 46.0% total return by roughly three-tenths and leaving it comfortably positive. That is the test that matters, and the rating survives it. The DCF value, before the roll-forward and the illiquidity haircut, is Rp5,770 per share.

Post-balance-sheet review. We searched for events after the 30 June 2026 balance sheet through 12 November 2026. The material item is the Pasar Rebo impairment: IDR87.0bn booked in September 2026, a non-cash write-down that takes net book value to IDR75.0bn against an appraised market value of IDR93.0bn [S5]. It reduces equity and book value and touches neither cash nor free cash flow, so nothing is added to the valuation bridge; it is disclosed here and in the financial section rather than in the earnings path. The 8 October 2026 public expose set out the contract end and the export plan but disclosed no new debt, divestment, acquisition or special dividend [S2][S6]. The FY2025 dividend was declared in May 2026, before the balance-sheet date, and is not a post-date item [S3]. The bridge is empty because there is nothing to bridge, not because we did not look.

The cross-checks now do their proper job, which is to say what the market pays rather than what we would like it to pay. At Rp3,490 the shares trade on 4.2x the last clean contract year's earnings and 8.9x the first post-contract year's [S0]. The engine prints two EV multiples and they are struck on different balance sheets, which has to be spelled out because the earlier draft set them side by side as one series. 3.7x trailing EBITDA pairs the FY2025A result, which already contains one quarter of the repriced contract, with the FY2025A balance sheet: it is a spot multiple and it is correct. 3.7x pairs the first post-contract year's EBITDA with the net cash the model forecasts for that same year, so it credits cash the company has not earned yet and flatters the price. On one balance sheet — the 30 June 2026 net cash, about a fifth of the market value — that same post-contract EBITDA is six and a half times and the same operating profit is just under seven times [S0]. That is roughly two-thirds more expensive than the forward figure, and it is still not expensive for a business with almost no debt, a high return on a written-down asset base and a prescription franchise growing ahead of its market. What it is not is the story the earlier draft told. We are not going to dress six and a half times post-cliff profit as expensive. The honest question is the reverse one: what would have to be true for the market to be right, and is that more probable than our base case? The DCF answers it by construction, because it discounts the peak as a dated stream and then values the franchise that is left. A reader who insists on an earnings multiple as the primary method is making the same bet in a cruder form: applying today's post-contract multiple to the post-contract year returns the price by construction, so the multiple leg cannot corroborate the DCF, it can only show what the market assumes. The DCF's claim is that the franchise is worth more than the market's post-cliff multiple; the only ways it is wrong are if the post-contract earnings are lower than we model, the cash is not reachable, or the discount rate is much higher. Those are the three questions in the risk section.

Sensitivity. The inputs that carry most of the value are the size of the revenue step-down in FY2028E, the gross margin and cost ratio on the prescription business after the contract ends, and the cost of capital. The first is the one we know least about, and it is the reason the bear case is a genuine alternative rather than a formality. The table below runs the discount rate and the terminal growth rate around our base; the scenario table in the risk section runs the operating inputs, where two percentage points on the post-contract margin is worth more than half a point on the discount rate. A market-wide re-rating of Indonesian small caps would swamp both, which is why we do not present the sensitivity as a range of targets.

What the price implies. Running the DCF backwards at Rp3,490 produces an answer with a period attached to it: a -14.3% change to the revenue growth rate in every forecast year is what makes the model's value equal the price, which puts implied FY2027E revenue growth at -9.3% against the 5.0% we assume [S0]. That is a strong statement. It says the market is not pricing our cliff and a recovery; it is pricing a worse cliff, or no recovery, or a discount rate well above ours. A company whose prescription sales grew 7.7% against a market growing 6.2% [S2] does not obviously deserve that. The plainest reading, and the one the earlier draft avoided, is that a 12.5% float in a micro-cap controlled by a single shareholder trades at a structural discount that has little to do with the next decade's cash flow: a buyer of size cannot get in or out, and the controller sets the dividend. That is a reason the shares are cheap; it is not a reason they will stop being cheap, and it is why the target carries the full illiquidity haircut rather than a gesture at one.

Indonesian small-cap pharmaceutical distributors have historically traded at a discount to the
regional sector because of thin free floats, concentrated ownership and the difficulty foreign
institutions face in building positions. That discount has widened and narrowed with the rupiah
rather than with earnings, which is why we treat the discount rate as a range rather than a point.

The largest risk is the one the model already contains, and its size is uncertain rather than its existence: the tolling book leaves on 31 December 2027 and no source discloses how large it is [S5][S6]. Our base now sizes it at roughly a third of FY2027E sales, derived from the sourced price step rather than assumed, so the risk is that the true share is higher and the FY2028E trough deeper. Likelihood medium to high, impact material.

The second risk is transfer pricing, and it should be quantified rather than gestured at. About 60.0% of Healthcare sales are imported biotech products bought from the parent [S2]. Those imports are the bulk of cost of goods, so related-party purchases are of the order of half to two-thirds of group cost of goods and around a third of revenue by the time they are sold. The price at which they are transferred determines the local margin, and the parent is on both sides of the transaction and controls the board. We found no evidence of abuse: the company reports a return on equity of 11.6% and pays a substantial dividend [S2][S3]. But the mechanism is unobservable from outside, it is the channel the earnings-quality card tells us to weight most heavily on this exchange, and the visible regulatory trend points the same way. Likelihood medium, impact high, unhedgeable.

The third risk is liquidity and ownership. The free float is 12.5% on the registry's basis and three-month average daily traded value is only about 104,688,444 rupiah a day [S0]. For a fund of any size this is not an investable position at scale, and the price at which a seller transacts can differ materially from the modelled value. There is corporate-action risk in both directions: a controlling shareholder with this stake can pursue a voluntary delisting or a squeeze-out at a price minorities may consider unfair, and equally could move product rights to another group company. Likelihood low to medium, impact high. It is the reason the target carries the full illiquidity haircut, not a reason to add another premium somewhere else.

Inside that risk sits a dated one the earlier draft missed: the float is below the exchange's minimum of 15.0% of shares outstanding for continued listing [S7]. The phase-in runs by market capitalisation, and an issuer of this size has until 31 March 2029 to reach the threshold [S7]. The same circular also gives a shorter deadline to issuers whose free float sits between twelve and a half and fifteen per cent, who must comply by 31 March 2027 [S7]; Merck's 12.5% float falls inside that band as well as inside the below-five-trillion-rupiah tier, so on that reading the equity event lands within our holding period rather than after it. We do not know which reading the exchange will apply to this issuer, and we flag it rather than assume the later date: whether the event is a parent sell-down or a placement, the per-share effect described below is unchanged, and we would revisit the share count on any announcement. The company can only close a gap of roughly two and a half points in one of two ways, and both change the per-share arithmetic. The parent can sell down, which is neutral for value but relieves the discount the shares carry; or the company can issue new shares, which is value-neutral to the enterprise and dilutive to existing holders at this price. A placement at the current discount is the more likely route for a controlled issuer that wants to keep the parent at the helm, and it is a real risk to the per-share target even where it is irrelevant to the value of the business. We do not model it because neither the size nor the timing is disclosed; we flag it as a structural risk with a hard deadline, and we would revisit the share count on any announcement. Likelihood of an equity event before the deadline: medium; impact on per-share value: dilutive, and larger the wider the discount to intrinsic value at which the shares are placed.

The fourth risk is the rupiah. The imported majority of the portfolio is dollar-cost, rupiah-revenue, so a depreciation episode compresses gross margin until prices are reset [S6]. The house macro deck has the rupiah at 18,350 against 17,968 spot and 19,000 in the long run, so the direction is against us. We do not shock it in the scenarios because a currency shock and a margin shock would be the same shock counted twice; it is in the cost base and in the country risk premium instead. Likelihood high, impact moderate.

The fifth risk is operational and regulatory: the export plan depends on qualifying Pasar Rebo for multiple jurisdictions on a timetable the company set out publicly [S6], and slippage delays the replacement of the tolling profit. Alongside it sits portfolio concentration: a handful of molecules carry the prescription business, and a single loss of exclusivity or a reimbursement decision could remove a meaningful share of profit. Neither is modelled as a shock because neither can be sized from the disclosures; both are in the bear case implicitly, through lower prescription growth and a lower post-contract margin. Likelihood medium, impact moderate to high.

The sixth risk is the one minorities should think about hardest, and it is about access to the cash rather than the existence of it. Net cash is IDR-349.6bn, which is a large share of the market value [S0], and the valuation credits it in full because it is on the balance sheet and unencumbered. But a minority holder cannot draw it. What a minority actually receives before the cliff is the dividend: we model Rp391 and Rp417 per share in the two contract years at the assumed payout, and that, not the cash pile, is the realistic cash return. The parent could upstream the same value through transfer pricing instead of dividends, which is legal, disclosed at the group level and invisible in the local accounts. Likelihood low to medium, impact material, and it is the reason we do not capitalise the net cash at more than its book value.

Scenarios are mirrored on the same three drivers, and the long-run growth rate is not shocked. That is deliberate: the earlier draft pushed the perpetual tail up three points in the bull case, which turned a small revenue assumption into half again the value and made the probability-weighted target a leverage on a modelling artefact. The bear and bull now move revenue growth by two points, gross margin by two points and the cost ratio by two points in opposite directions, and nothing else. The bear case takes 35.0% and assumes the tolling book is larger than we model, prescription growth fades toward the market rate, and the odds of the cost block leaving with the contract are given against us. The bull case takes 20.0% and assumes the prescription franchise holds its recent pace, the ASEAN exports qualify on schedule, and the consumer-health cost block does leave with the revenue. The base case carries 45.0% because it is the most probable path, not a cautious one: it reproduces the last actual's economics in the contract years and then lets the prescription business stand on its own.

The asymmetry is worth stating in numbers the engine produces. The bear DCF value is Rp4,404 and the base Rp5,770, both above the Rp3,490 share price; the bull is Rp7,511. A reader who thinks the bear case deserves half the probability should notice that the bear case is still a good outcome at this price, which is a stronger statement about the valuation than any probability we could assign.

Where the optimism in this report actually sits, stated plainly, is the tail and the post-contract cost base. The explicit years do not carry the claim: the tolling cash flow is contract-dated and the FY2028E trough is modelled. The tail does, and so does the decision to hold SG&A at the last actual's share of prescription revenue rather than let it fall as the export volumes scale. Both are defensible and sourced as judgments, and both would be attacked by a reader who believes a controlled micro-cap with a narrow moat should be valued on a fade. Our answer is the tail test in the valuation section rather than a claim: reprice the perpetuity at the multiple the market pays today and the target falls by about a tenth but stays above the price. If that judgment is wrong, the failure shows up first in the post-contract SG&A ratio and second in the terminal multiple, not in the contract years.

Signposts that would change the view. A disclosure of the tolling revenue split in the FY2026 annual report would resolve the central uncertainty; we would raise the target if the share is smaller than we derive and cut it if larger. A declaration that the parent intends to inject products or consolidate the Indonesian entity would change the governance assessment rather than the cash flow. A dividend cut larger than the payout we assume would signal that the transition is being funded from the balance sheet rather than from cash flow, which would cut the value of the net cash leg. And any evidence of related-party pricing moving against the listed entity would be a kill signal, not a rating change.

Ownership is concentrated to the point where minority holders are along for the ride. Merck Holding GmbH's stake is the pack's 91.3% insider line; the institutions line of 2.5% and the registry's free float of 12.5% are counted on different bases and cannot be added to it, as the business section sets out [S0]. The practical reading is a single controller with an overwhelming majority of the votes and a float of about an eighth of the shares. That float is below the exchange's 15.0% minimum for continued listing, with a phase-in to 31 March 2029 for issuers of this size, or 31 March 2027 on the register's alternative reading for the twelve-and-a-half to fifteen per cent float band [S7]; the company is therefore on a timetable to an equity event, whether a parent sell-down or a new issue, and that is a governance fact rather than a forecast. The board is management-heavy, with the president director also carrying the biopharma portfolio and a finance director drawn from the group [S0]. There is no evidence in the sources we obtained of pledged shares, of a special-monitoring-board designation, or of the special notation letters that would signal going-concern or reporting problems; the FY2025 accounts were approved at the annual meeting in May 2026, where the dividend was also approved [S3]. That is an absence of adverse evidence, not a verification: we could not obtain the audited accounts or the auditor's opinion for this report, and we flag it as a gap rather than assert a clean bill of health.

Related-party exposure is the central governance fact of this company and it is structural, not incidental. The parent is the supplier of the imported majority of the portfolio, the owner of the product licences, the controlling shareholder and the counterparty on group accounting policy; the plant impairment itself was booked on Merck Group accounting guidance as well as the local standard [S5][S2]. The company does not disclose the share of purchases or sales with related parties in the material we obtained, which is itself a disclosure gap on a name where the parent is the main supplier [S5]. Minority holders therefore depend on the parent's pricing discipline for their economics. The dividend record is the best available counter-evidence: the company has paid a substantial dividend every year in the pack history, including IDR123.2bn for FY2025, which is Rp275 per share [S3][S0]. A controlling shareholder intent on starving minorities would not distribute at that rate.

The dividend trajectory is worth stating precisely because it is a signal, but only the part of it we can source. The payout was about half of FY2025 net profit after a much higher proportion in FY2024 [S3][S0], and that step is already the board's own response to the contract end rather than a forecast of our own. Beyond it we found no dividend guidance in any source, so the flat payout we carry is our assumption, disclosed as such in the financial section. A reader should treat the dividend as the main channel through which a minority participates in the net cash, and the payout ratio as the variable the board controls.

ESG exposures are those of a mid-sized pharmaceutical manufacturer in Jakarta. The material issues are product quality and pharmacovigilance, access to medicines in a reimbursed market, and the environmental footprint of the Pasar Rebo plant, which sits in a dense urban area and has just been written down partly on utilisation grounds [S5]. The company discloses a compliance officer and a legal function in its leadership list [S0], which is thin disclosure by regional standards; we found no sustainability report and no emissions or water disclosure. On the social side, the pivot to local manufacture of oral antidiabetics for domestic and regional supply is a genuine access story rather than a marketing one, and it is the part of the strategy we would most like to see quantified [S6]. On governance we record three evidence gaps rather than assume them away: no auditor opinion was obtainable, no related-party transaction schedule was disclosed in the material we could fetch, and no IDX board or notation status was verifiable from the sources available to a research desk that cannot cite the exchange. None of the three shows anything adverse; all three are absences, and an absence is not a clean bill of health.

The calendar is unusually clean because the company has dated its own transition. The Philippines export shipments are targeted for 2026 and are the first test of whether the plant can replace tolling volume with prescription volume [S6]. The FY2026 audited accounts, due in the first quarter of 2027, are the first clean annual read on the repriced contract margin and should disclose the segment split we are missing [S3]. The FY2027 meeting is the last dividend declaration before the contract ends, and it will tell us how the board intends to bridge the cliff [S3][S5]. The contract itself expires on 31 December 2027, after which the first full post-contract year will be reported in early 2028 [S5].

Between updates we watch four things: the quarterly gross margin and its fourth-quarter true-up, which tells us whether the contractual margin is being delivered as modelled [S0]; the revenue split between prescription and manufacturing, which the annual report should disclose [S6]; the cash balance and payout, which together determine how much of the net cash survives the transition [S0]; and any related-party disclosure around imported product pricing or group restructuring [S5]. We would revisit the rating on any of these moving materially against the model, and we would treat a squeeze-out proposal as a separate event requiring a fresh valuation rather than an update.
